newsitem.title: UK: UK petrol tax will not put motorists in reverse.
newsitem.headline: UK petrol tax will not put motorists in reverse.

text.p: Britain's 29 million motorists will dig deeper into their pockets to buy petrol after the July 2 budget but it will still not be expensive enough for them to leave their cars at home and take public transport, energy industry sources said.
That's because pump prices in Britain are in the basement of European rankings and consumers find buses and trains too inconvenient for local trips or holidays.
Long-term measures aimed at using alternative fuels and discouraging company cars could, however, help the Labour government meet its targets on reducing carbon dioxide emissions, the sources said.
Company vehicles are eight percent of the country's 22 million cars, the Automobile Association says.

"Demand is pretty much inelastic and previous attempts to do this have not been successful because people value their personal mobility quite highly," said Stephen Brooks, principal consultant at Wood Mackenzie in Edinburgh.
"You have to have a significant hike in prices to really have an impact on journey patterns and car usage and the levels at which we're talking about...are not (significant) in themselves," he said.
"If they were to apply (measures) on a consistent and regular basis it may have a marginal negative impact on the oil industry."
Chancellor Gordon Brown in his first budget is expected to raise the fuel duty by at least five percent, above the rate of inflation, the sources predicted.

That could translate into an increase of three to four pence per litre on top of the average premium unleaded price of 59 pence per litre, sources said. Taxes already grab more than three-quarters of the price.
The AA predicted the vehicle excise duty may also rise to 150-155 sterling from 145 sterling and the Insurance Premium Tax (IPT) from four percent to possibly as high as 12.5 or 17.5 pct.
The AA outlined in a 20-page pre-budget brief that for every one pence per gallon increase in motor fuel duty, including the value added tax, the treasury receives an extra 60 million sterling.
A motorist driving 8,000 miles a year would pay 40 sterling more on unleaded petrol a year if the minimum likely increase is introduced, it said.

"Dramatic increases in fuel duty...will not lead to a decrease in traffic -- 82 percent of motorists say that they will still use their cars even if petrol prices double over 10 years," the group said.

"The car is not a luxury in most people's lives, it is essential," it said. "Increased motoring costs will hit lower- and middle-income motorists first, leading to a socially divisive 'roads for the rich' situation."

British Prime Minister Tony Blair at a United Nations conference on Monday committed to cutting the country's emissions of carbon dioxide, the main greenhouse gas, by 20 percent from 1990 levels by 2010 and said sweeping lifestyle changes would be needed to hit the target.

He ruled out at the weekend new environmental taxes but officials said the government was working on a broad range of measures including more bus lanes, energy efficiency schemes and improved traffic management.

Motorists have enjoyed the consequences of a petrol price war since early 1996 when Esso Petroleum, a unit of U.S. oil giant Exxon Corp, launched its Pricewatch campaign promising to match its lowest-priced competitors, in this case the supermarket chains.
The UK Petroleum Industry Association hopes the government will take into account the unequal taxing structure between the oil companies and the hypermarkets.

The major oil companies in the 13-member PIA lost 110 million sterling in 1996 after a profit of 94 million sterling in 1995, a worrying result that Michael Frend, Director General of the PIA, hopes the government will address.
"All the indications are that Blair will introduce higher tax on fuels than the five percent above inflation," he said.

"As an industry we find that a very blunt instrument in trying to have an impact on environmental problems such as carbon dioxide emissions...If you increase the price it has very little impact on consumption."
Higher taxes and incentives for alternative fuels would be welcomed by some environmental groups.
"We're very encouraged by the positive messages coming across from the government," said Chris Brown, head of public affairs at the Energy Saving Trust.

The group, established by the government and electric and gas companies in response to the 1992 Earth Summit in Rio de Janeiro, hoped for a reduction in the value added tax on energy saving materials.

"Whatever tax increase comes out in motor fuels next week will have to be looked at in the overall context of the transportation sector," said Robert Olle, a director of independent analysts Oil Price Assessments Ltd (OPAL).
